short: Short for financial technology: companies and software that use apps, data and the internet to deliver payments, lending, investing or insurance.
kid: Long ago, you had to walk to a big building to send coins to a friend. Now a phone can do it in a blink. Fintech is all the clever phone tricks that help people pay for things and look after their pocket money.
detail: Fintech, short for financial technology, means using software, mobile apps, data and cloud computing to deliver financial services faster, more cheaply or to more people. It covers payments (UPI apps, wallets, payment gateways), digital lending, online broking and wealth apps, insurtech, regtech and the systems banks themselves run on. India has one of the world's largest fintech ecosystems, built on public digital rails such as Aadhaar, UPI and account aggregators, with firms like PhonePe, Paytm, Razorpay and Zerodha. Regulators matter as much as code: the RBI, SEBI and IRDAI decide which activities need a licence, and the RBI runs a regulatory sandbox for testing new ideas. Common confusion: many fintechs are not banks or lenders themselves; they partner with licensed banks and NBFCs, which hold the deposits and carry the loans on their books.
example: Say a hypothetical payments start-up, XYZ Pay, handles 50 lakh merchant payments a month and earns ₹0.50 on each. That is ₹25 lakh of revenue a month, or ₹3 crore a year, from fees that are tiny per payment but large at scale.

short: India's instant payment system that moves money between bank accounts 24x7 using a phone app, a UPI ID or a QR code.
kid: Imagine you could send a sweet to your friend's lunchbox just by pointing your phone at a little picture. It gets there in a blink, any time of day. This does the same with pocket money.
detail: The Unified Payments Interface is a real-time payment system built and run by the National Payments Corporation of India and launched in 2016. It lets a user link bank accounts to a mobile app and pay anyone instantly using a virtual payment address (such as name@bank), a mobile number or a QR code, approving each payment with a UPI PIN. Money moves directly from bank account to bank account, round the clock; apps such as PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm and BHIM are only front ends. UPI is free for users, and under the rules as of 2025 merchants pay no merchant discount rate on ordinary UPI payments, which helped it become India's dominant retail payment mode, handling billions of transactions a month. Common confusion: UPI is not an app or a wallet; it is the shared rail every app plugs into.
example: Say Riya pays ₹250 at a tea stall by scanning its UPI QR code and entering her PIN. Within seconds ₹250 leaves her bank account and lands in the stall owner's, with no fee to either side under the rules as of 2025. If she makes 40 such payments in a month, she moves ₹10,000 without touching cash.

short: A small on-phone balance within UPI for quick, low-value payments that go through without entering a UPI PIN each time.
kid: It is like keeping a few coins in your pocket for sweets, instead of opening your big piggy bank every time. You just tap and go.
detail: UPI Lite, launched by NPCI in 2022, lets a user move a small amount from a bank account into an on-device balance inside a UPI app and then make small payments from it without entering the UPI PIN. Under the rules as of 2025, each payment can be up to ₹1,000 and the balance up to ₹5,000, with optional automatic top-ups. Because these payments are recorded against the Lite balance instead of hitting the bank's core system every time, they fail less often at peak hours, and the bank statement shows only the top-ups rather than dozens of tiny entries. UPI Lite X, announced in 2023, adds offline phone-to-phone payments using NFC. Common confusion: UPI Lite is not a separate wallet company; the money stays with your own bank. But anyone holding your unlocked phone could spend it, which is why the balance is capped low.
example: Say Arjun loads ₹2,000 into UPI Lite and buys five snacks at ₹120 each without a PIN. He spends ₹600, leaving ₹1,400, and his bank statement shows a single ₹2,000 top-up instead of five separate debits.

short: The not-for-profit company, set up by the RBI and banks, that runs India's shared retail payment systems such as UPI, RuPay and IMPS.
kid: Think of the people who build and look after the roads so every delivery van can reach every house. This group builds the roads that let pocket money travel from one friend to another.
detail: The National Payments Corporation of India is the umbrella organisation for retail payments, set up in 2008 under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, at the initiative of the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks' Association. It is a not-for-profit company owned by banks. NPCI builds and operates shared rails that every bank and app can plug into: UPI, IMPS, RuPay, NACH, AePS, the toll system behind FASTag and the cheque truncation system, while subsidiaries run the Bharat Bill Payment System and take UPI and RuPay abroad. Its rules, for example on transaction limits or app market share, shape the whole payments industry. Common confusion: NPCI is not the regulator; the RBI authorises and supervises it. Also, NEFT and RTGS are run by the RBI itself, not by NPCI.
example: Say UPI handles 2,000 crore transactions in a month. Under the 30% market-share cap NPCI set for UPI apps, whose deadline had been pushed to the end of 2026 under the rules as of 2025, no single app could process more than 600 crore of them.

short: An Indian system for instant bank-to-bank transfers, available 24x7, that sends money using the receiver's account number and branch code.
kid: Imagine a magic slide between two piggy banks. You drop a coin in one, and it lands in the other right away, even at night.
detail: Immediate Payment Service, launched by NPCI in 2010, is an instant interbank transfer system available round the clock, including holidays, through mobile banking, internet banking, ATMs and branches. The sender usually identifies the receiver by account number and IFSC, and the payee is credited within seconds; the banks then settle their net positions with each other in several cycles a day. Under the rules as of 2025, the per-transaction limit is ₹5 lakh, and banks may charge a small fee. IMPS was the rail on which UPI was later built, and it remains popular for one-off transfers to accounts not on UPI and for amounts above UPI's usual cap. Common confusion: NEFT also runs 24x7 now, but it settles in half-hourly batches, whereas IMPS credits each payment individually and instantly.
example: Say you need to send ₹3 lakh to a relative at 11 pm on a Sunday. Under the rules as of 2025 that is above UPI's usual ₹1 lakh limit but within IMPS's ₹5 lakh limit, so a single IMPS transfer can deliver the full amount within seconds.

short: An RBI-run system for moving money between Indian bank accounts, processed in half-hourly batches round the clock, with no minimum amount.
kid: Think of a school bus that leaves every half hour. Everyone's notes for friends ride the bus together and get delivered at the next stop.
detail: National Electronic Funds Transfer is a nationwide payment system owned and operated by the Reserve Bank of India for one-to-one bank transfers. Instead of settling each payment on its own, NEFT collects instructions and settles them in half-hourly batches on a deferred net basis, so banks exchange only their net amounts in each batch. Since December 2019 it has run 24x7, all year, with 48 batches a day, and the receiving bank must credit the beneficiary within two hours of a batch settling. The RBI sets no minimum or maximum amount, and online NEFT is free for savings account holders under the rules as of 2025. It suits rent, salaries and supplier payments where a short wait is fine. Common confusion: 24x7 does not mean instant; NEFT is batch-based, unlike IMPS or RTGS.
example: Say you send ₹2 lakh of rent by NEFT at 10:10 am. It joins the 10:30 am batch, and the landlord's bank must credit it within two hours of that batch settling, so the money should land by about 12:30 pm. With a batch every 30 minutes, there are 24 x 2 = 48 batches a day.

short: An RBI-run system for large bank transfers in which each payment is settled one by one, instantly and finally, rather than in batches.
kid: Imagine handing a big, heavy box straight to your friend, one box at a time, instead of waiting to pile them all into a van. Once it is in their hands, it is theirs for good.
detail: Real Time Gross Settlement is the Reserve Bank of India's system for high-value transfers. Real time means payments are processed continuously as they arrive; gross means each one is settled individually and in full, not netted against other payments. Settlement happens in central bank money on the RBI's books, so it is final and irrevocable. RTGS has run 24x7 since December 2020, and under the rules as of 2025 the minimum is ₹2 lakh with no upper limit. Because banks need enough balance for every payment, the RBI offers intraday liquidity against collateral. Similar systems include Fedwire in the US, CHAPS in the UK and T2 in the euro area. Common confusion: RTGS settles instantly between banks; IMPS and UPI credit customers instantly, but the banks settle net amounts later.
example: Say Bank X owes Bank Y ₹100 crore during the day and Bank Y owes Bank X ₹90 crore. A net system would settle just ₹10 crore at the end of a cycle, but RTGS moves the full ₹100 crore and ₹90 crore separately, each the moment it is sent, so neither bank is left waiting on the other.

short: Payment systems that move money between accounts within seconds, round the clock, like UPI in India, Pix in Brazil and FedNow in the US.
kid: Some letters take days to arrive. This is like whispering in your friend's ear: they hear it right away, even at bedtime.
detail: Real-time payments, also called instant or fast payments, are account-to-account transfers in which the payee can use the money within seconds, 24x7, with immediate confirmation to both sides. Examples include the UK's Faster Payments (2008), India's IMPS and UPI, Brazil's Pix (launched by its central bank in 2020), the US Federal Reserve's FedNow (2023) and Europe's SEPA Instant. India processes the largest share of the world's real-time payments by volume. These systems cut the need for cash and cheques, speed up cash flow for small businesses and give central banks a public alternative to card networks. Common confusion: instant for the customer does not always mean instant between banks. FedNow settles each payment individually, but UPI and IMPS credit customers at once while banks settle net amounts later in the day.
example: Say a US plumber finishes a $1,200 job at 9 pm on a Saturday and the customer pays through a bank that offers FedNow. The $1,200 is usable within seconds rather than after the weekend. If the plumber does 20 such jobs a month, $24,000 a month arrives the same day it is earned.

short: India's shared bill-payment network that lets you pay electricity, phone, gas, loan, card and other bills through any participating bank or app.
kid: Imagine one big post box in town where you can drop notes for the milk lady, the newspaper boy and the shop that fixes your lights, and every note reaches the right person.
detail: The Bharat Bill Payment System is an interoperable platform for recurring bill payments, mandated by the RBI and run by NPCI Bharat BillPay Ltd, an NPCI subsidiary. It connects thousands of billers, such as electricity boards, telecom and gas companies, lenders, insurers, schools and municipalities, to many customer-facing operating units, including banks and payment apps. Whichever app or agent outlet you use, the payment flows through the same central system, the biller is told at once, and you get a standard reference number and complaint process. RBI rules routed credit card bill payments through it from mid-2024, and the platform was rebranded Bharat Connect the same year. For billers, it cuts the cost of collecting from crores of small payers. Common confusion: BBPS is not an app; the apps showing its logo are front ends plugged into it.
example: Say you pay four bills in one sitting through a payments app: ₹1,850 for electricity, ₹499 for your phone, ₹650 for gas and ₹3,000 for a credit card, a total of ₹5,999. Each payment travels through BBPS, so each biller is informed at once and you get four reference numbers to quote if anything goes wrong.

short: An Indian system that lets people withdraw cash or check their balance at a local agent using only their Aadhaar number and fingerprint.
kid: Imagine a friendly shopkeeper who can hand you your own saved coins just by checking your fingerprint. No card, no secret number, just your finger.
detail: The Aadhaar Enabled Payment System, run by NPCI, lets a customer whose bank account is linked to Aadhaar carry out basic banking at a micro-ATM, usually a handheld device operated by a bank's business correspondent in a village shop. The customer gives their Aadhaar number, picks their bank and authenticates with a fingerprint or iris scan; services include cash withdrawal, cash deposit, balance enquiry, mini statements and Aadhaar-to-Aadhaar transfers. AePS matters for financial inclusion because many people receiving welfare payments and Direct Benefit Transfers live far from branches and ATMs. Its weak spot is fraud using cloned fingerprints, which is why UIDAI lets users lock their biometrics. Common confusion: AePS is for using money already in an Aadhaar-linked account; the Aadhaar Payment Bridge is the separate system that sends government benefits into those accounts.
example: Say a farmer receives a ₹2,000 PM-KISAN instalment, one of three a year that add up to ₹6,000 under the scheme as of 2025, in her Aadhaar-linked account. At the village micro-ATM she withdraws ₹1,500 with her fingerprint and leaves ₹500 in the account, without travelling to a branch.

short: A one-time digital permission that lets a company automatically collect a fixed or capped amount from your bank account, card or UPI on a schedule.
kid: It is like telling the milk lady she may take two coins from your jar every Monday. You say yes once, and you can change your mind any time.
detail: An e-mandate is a standing instruction, set up digitally, that authorises a merchant or lender to debit a customer's account, card or wallet on a recurring basis up to an agreed maximum and frequency. In India the main forms are NACH debit mandates (registered online as e-NACH through net banking, a debit card or Aadhaar), UPI AutoPay and card e-mandates. Under the RBI framework as of 2025, the customer authenticates when registering, gets a pre-debit notice at least 24 hours before each charge, can cancel at any time, and later debits run without fresh authentication up to ₹15,000, or ₹1 lakh for mutual fund SIPs, insurance premiums and credit card bills. Mandates power SIPs, loan EMIs and subscriptions. Common confusion: a mandate is permission, not money set aside; if the account is short on the date, the debit bounces and charges follow.
example: Say you start a ₹5,000 monthly SIP through UPI AutoPay. You enter your UPI PIN once to approve the mandate; after that ₹5,000 is debited each month without a PIN, following a notice the day before, so ₹60,000 goes into the fund over 12 months.

short: Paying by scanning a square barcode with your phone; the code tells your app whom to pay and sometimes how much.
kid: The shop puts up a little black-and-white picture. You point your phone at it, and your coins hop over to the shop.
detail: QR code payments let a customer pay by scanning a merchant's Quick Response code with a phone app, which reads the payee's details and starts a payment that the customer confirms. A static QR is printed once and the customer types the amount; a dynamic QR is generated for each bill with the amount filled in, which reduces errors. In India almost all such payments run on UPI QR codes, while Bharat QR, launched in 2017, also works with cards; the RBI has pushed interoperable codes so any app can pay any shop. Because a printed code costs almost nothing and UPI payments carry no merchant discount rate under the rules as of 2025, QR codes brought digital payments to street vendors. Common confusion, and a common scam: scanning a QR code is only ever for paying, never for receiving money.
example: Say a tea stall sells 200 cups a day at ₹15 each and every customer pays by scanning its UPI QR code. The stall receives ₹3,000 a day straight into its bank account and, under the rules as of 2025, pays no fee on it beyond the cost of printing the code.

short: Paying by tapping a card, phone or watch on a card machine, which reads it by short-range radio instead of a swipe or insert.
kid: You just touch your card to the shop's little box, like a high-five, and you are done.
detail: Contactless payments use near-field communication (NFC), a radio link that works only within a few centimetres, to pass payment data from a card, phone or wearable to a terminal. Each tap generates a one-time code, so the card's details are not exposed the way a magnetic-stripe swipe exposes them, and phone wallets add a token plus the phone's own lock. To keep checkout quick, small payments skip the PIN: in India, under the rules as of 2025, taps up to ₹5,000 need no PIN, and customers can switch contactless off or set a lower limit in their banking app. NFC also powers the offline payments of UPI Lite X. Common confusion: contactless is not an online payment; the card is physically present. The real risk is a lost card being tapped before it is blocked, which is why the no-PIN cap exists.
example: Say you tap your card for a ₹1,200 grocery bill and walk out without entering a PIN; a ₹6,500 bill would need a PIN under the rules as of 2025. If a lost card were tapped three times at ₹4,900 before being blocked, ₹14,700 would be at risk, which is why blocking a lost card quickly matters.

short: The place and device where a customer pays a shop, such as a card machine, a QR code stand or a payment soundbox.
kid: It is the counter where you hand over your coins and get your ice cream. Today there is often a little beeping box there to help.
detail: Point of sale (POS) is where a retail transaction is completed, and in payments it usually means the hardware at the counter: a POS terminal that reads cards by chip, swipe or tap and often shows UPI QR codes too, plus newer devices such as soundboxes that read out each UPI payment aloud. Terminals are supplied by an acquiring bank or payment aggregator, which charges the merchant a merchant discount rate on card payments, often a monthly rental too, and settles the money, usually the next working day. The RBI's Payments Infrastructure Development Fund, set up in 2021, has subsidised terminals in smaller towns and the north-east. Analysts also track POS data as a near-real-time read on consumer spending. Common confusion: a soundbox only announces payments; it does not take them. And point-of-sale finance is something else: credit offered at checkout.
example: Say a café takes ₹40,000 in card payments on its POS terminal in a day. At an MDR of, say, 1.5%, the acquirer keeps ₹600 and settles ₹39,400 into the café's account the next working day.

short: The technology at an online checkout that securely captures your payment details and passes them on for approval, then reports back yes or no.
kid: It is like the guard at a toy shop door who checks your ticket, whispers to the owner, and then says 'Come in!' or 'Sorry, not today.'
detail: A payment gateway is the software link between a website or app and the payment system. When a customer clicks pay, the gateway encrypts the card, UPI, net banking or wallet details, sends them through the acquirer and the card network or UPI switch to the customer's bank for authorisation, and returns the approval or decline to the merchant, usually within a couple of seconds. Gateways compete on success rates, speed, fraud screening and the range of payment methods offered. In India, the RBI's 2020 rules treat pure gateways as technology providers that need no licence, while payment aggregators, which handle merchants' money, need RBI authorisation. Common confusion: the two terms get mixed up because firms like Razorpay, PayU and Cashfree do both, but the gateway is the data pipe and the aggregator is the one holding and settling the funds.
example: Say an online shop sells a ₹2,499 item and gets 1,000 checkout attempts a day. If a better gateway lifts the payment success rate from 92% to 95%, 30 more orders go through each day, worth ₹74,970 in extra daily sales.

short: A firm that lets online shops accept many payment methods through one link, collects customers' money and passes it on to the shops.
kid: Imagine a big sister who collects coins from all the kids buying lemonade and then hands the whole jar to the lemonade stand at the end of the day.
detail: A payment aggregator signs up merchants, often small businesses that could not easily arrange card acceptance with a bank on their own, and lets them accept cards, UPI, net banking and wallets through a single integration. It collects customers' payments into its own account and settles them to the merchant, minus fees. Because it holds other people's money in transit, the RBI has regulated aggregators since 2020: non-bank aggregators need RBI authorisation, must keep customer funds in an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank, must check merchants' KYC and, under the rules as of 2025, must have a net worth of at least ₹15 crore when applying and ₹25 crore by the end of the third year. The rules were later extended to offline and cross-border aggregators. Common confusion: the aggregator holds and settles funds, while a payment gateway only carries payment data.
example: Say a small online store, ABC Crafts, sells ₹1,00,000 of goods in a day through an aggregator charging 2%. The ₹1,00,000 lands in the aggregator's escrow account; the aggregator keeps ₹2,000 as its fee (ignoring GST) and settles ₹98,000 to the store, typically the next working day.

short: An app that stores money you load in advance, or your saved cards, so you can pay from your phone without cash.
kid: It is like a little purse inside your phone. You put some coins in first, then you can spend them on sweets by tapping your phone.
detail: A digital wallet is a phone or online account used to pay, and it comes in two kinds. Stored-value wallets hold money loaded in advance; in India the RBI calls these prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), a group that also covers gift cards and metro cards, issued by banks and RBI-authorised non-banks. Under the rules as of 2025, full-KYC wallets can hold up to ₹2 lakh, minimum-KYC wallets far less, and full-KYC wallets must work across UPI. Pass-through wallets such as Apple Pay or Google Wallet hold no money; they store tokenised versions of your cards. Common confusion: wallet money is not a bank deposit. It earns no interest and is not covered by deposit insurance, so it relies on the issuer's safeguards; the RBI's 2024 curbs on Paytm Payments Bank showed that an issuer can be barred from taking new top-ups.
example: Say you load ₹5,000 into a wallet, then spend ₹1,250 on a metro pass and ₹890 on a food order. Your balance is ₹2,860, and unlike money in a savings account, it earns no interest while it sits there.

short: A company such as Visa, Mastercard or RuPay that runs the system connecting the banks that issue cards with the shops that accept them.
kid: Imagine a long telephone wire that lets your piggy bank talk to the toy shop's till, so the shop knows your coins are real.
detail: A card network, or card scheme, operates the messaging, clearing and settlement system behind card payments and writes the rules every participant follows. In the four-party model used by Visa, Mastercard and RuPay, the issuer is the cardholder's bank, the acquirer is the merchant's bank or aggregator, and the network routes the authorisation request between them, settles the money and sets interchange fees. The network earns fees on volume and processing; it does not lend or carry the credit risk. In a three-party model, such as American Express, the network also issues cards and signs up merchants itself. China UnionPay is the largest by cards issued. In India, RBI rules from 2024 require card issuers to let eligible customers choose their network. Common confusion: the logo on your card is not your lender; your bank is.
example: Say you pay ₹10,000 at an electronics store with a Visa card. The terminal sends the request through the store's acquirer to Visa, which routes it to your bank for approval in a second or two. If the store's MDR is, say, 1.8%, it receives ₹9,820, and the ₹180 is split among your bank, Visa and the acquirer.

short: India's home-grown card network, used for debit, credit and prepaid cards across Indian shops, ATMs and websites, and linkable to UPI.
kid: Some cards come from big companies in faraway lands. This one was made at home in India, for everyone in India.
detail: RuPay is a domestic card network launched by NPCI in 2012 as an Indian alternative to Visa and Mastercard. Because processing stays within India, it is cheaper for banks, and RuPay debit cards went to crores of Jan Dhan account holders. Under the rules as of 2025, merchants pay no merchant discount rate on RuPay debit card payments, just as with UPI from bank accounts. Since 2022, RuPay credit cards can be linked to UPI, so a customer can pay at any UPI QR code from a credit line; merchants generally pay an MDR on these payments, and the issuing bank earns interchange. For acceptance abroad, RuPay partners with networks such as JCB and Discover. Common confusion: RuPay is a network, not a bank; the card is still issued by your bank, which sets your limit, fees and interest.
example: Say you pay ₹1,800 at a shop's UPI QR code using a RuPay credit card linked to UPI. Nothing leaves your bank account that day; the ₹1,800 goes on your card statement. If you make 10 such payments in a month, ₹18,000 is billed together, and paying the full bill by the due date means no interest.

short: A fee the shop's bank pays the cardholder's bank on every card payment; it is the largest part of what shops pay to accept cards.
kid: When you buy a toy with a special ticket, the shop gives a tiny crumb of its cookie to the friend who gave you that ticket. That crumb is a thank-you.
detail: An interchange fee is paid by the acquirer, the merchant's bank or payment aggregator, to the issuer, the cardholder's bank, on each card transaction. The card network sets it, usually as a percentage of the value, sometimes plus a small fixed amount, and it varies by card type, merchant category and channel: premium credit cards, corporate cards and online payments carry higher rates than debit cards. Issuers use interchange to pay for rewards, fraud losses and interest-free periods, which is why generous reward cards exist. Because merchants bear it inside the merchant discount rate, it is a regulatory target: under the rules as of 2025, the EU caps consumer card interchange at 0.2% for debit and 0.3% for credit, and the US caps debit interchange for large banks. Common confusion: merchants do not pay interchange directly; they pay the MDR to their acquirer, which passes interchange to the issuer.
example: Say a customer spends $100 on a credit card. If interchange is 1.8%, the issuer gets $1.80; add a network fee of $0.15 and an acquirer margin of $0.35, and the merchant pays $2.30 in all, an MDR of 2.3%, receiving $97.70.
formula: Interchange fee = Transaction value x Interchange rate (+ fixed fee per transaction, if any)

short: The fee a shop pays, as a percentage of each sale, to the bank or firm that lets it accept card or digital payments.
kid: When a helper carries your lemonade coins to your jar, they keep one little coin as a thank-you. That little coin is this.
detail: The merchant discount rate is the charge a merchant pays its acquiring bank or payment aggregator for processing a digital payment, expressed as a percentage of the transaction value. It bundles three pieces: the interchange fee paid to the card issuer, the network's scheme fee and the acquirer's own margin. Credit cards, especially premium and international ones, usually cost merchants more than debit cards. In India, the government made UPI payments from bank accounts and RuPay debit card payments zero-MDR from January 2020, which still holds under the rules as of 2025; instead, the government pays banks an incentive on small UPI merchant payments. Zero MDR helped small shops adopt UPI but squeezes the revenue of payment companies, a long-running industry debate. Common confusion: MDR is not the same as interchange; interchange is only the issuer's slice of the MDR.
example: Say a shop takes ₹50,000 in credit card payments at an MDR of 1.8%. It pays ₹900 and receives ₹49,100. Had the same ₹50,000 come through UPI from customers' bank accounts, under the rules as of 2025 it would pay no MDR and receive the full ₹50,000.
formula: MDR (%) = Merchant fee / Transaction value x 100; MDR = Interchange + Network fee + Acquirer margin

short: A forced reversal of a card payment, made by the cardholder's bank after the customer disputes the charge, pulling money back from the merchant.
kid: If you pay for a toy and it never comes, a grown-up can step in and make the shop give your coins back.
detail: A chargeback happens when a cardholder disputes a transaction with their issuing bank, for example over fraud, goods not delivered, goods not as described or a duplicate charge, and the issuer reverses the payment through the card network, taking the money back from the merchant's acquirer. Networks set strict reason codes and deadlines, often around 120 days. The merchant can contest with evidence such as proof of delivery, a step called representment, and the network may arbitrate. Merchants also pay chargeback fees, and those with high chargeback ratios face penalties or can lose the ability to accept cards, so the ratio is a key risk metric for e-commerce firms and payment aggregators. UPI has its own dispute process. Common confusion: a refund is given voluntarily by the merchant; a chargeback is forced through the banking system, usually after the merchant would not or could not fix the problem.
example: Say a customer pays ₹8,000 online for a jacket that the courier loses, and the merchant ignores her complaints. She disputes the charge, the bank reverses the ₹8,000, and the merchant also pays a chargeback fee of, say, ₹500. Having already shipped a jacket that cost it ₹3,000, the merchant ends up ₹3,500 worse off than if it had never made the sale.

short: Replacing your real card number with a unique stand-in code, so shops and apps never need to store the actual number.
kid: Instead of giving the shop your real house key, you give them a special key that only opens one door in one shop. If someone steals it, your house is still safe.
detail: Card tokenisation replaces the 16-digit card number with a token, a substitute number that works only for a specific merchant, device or app and is useless anywhere else. The card network or issuer acts as the token service provider and keeps the mapping in a secure vault; the merchant stores only the token. In India, RBI rules made card-on-file tokenisation (CoFT) mandatory from 1 October 2022: merchants and aggregators may no longer store customers' full card numbers, so saving a card on a shopping site now creates a token, with the customer's consent and an extra authentication step. Phone wallets such as Apple Pay and Google Wallet use device tokens. A data breach at a merchant therefore exposes tokens, not cards. Common confusion: card tokenisation is not encryption, and it has nothing to do with crypto tokens or the tokenisation of real-world assets on a blockchain.
example: Say you save the same card, ending 4321, on three shopping sites. Each site gets a different token. If one of the three sites is hacked, the thief gets a token that works only on that site, and you can delete that one token without blocking the card or touching the other two.

short: An extra check, beyond your card details or password, that proves a payment is really yours, such as a one-time password or fingerprint.
kid: Before the treehouse door opens, you say the secret word and also show your special badge. Two checks keep strangers out.
detail: An additional factor of authentication is a second, independent proof of identity needed before a digital payment goes through. Factors come in three kinds: something you know (a PIN or password), something you have (a registered phone that gets a one-time password) and something you are (a fingerprint or face). Since 2009 the RBI has required one for online card payments, hence the familiar OTP, while UPI pairs the bound phone with the UPI PIN. RBI directions issued in 2025, effective from April 2026, extend two-factor checks to digital payments broadly, require at least one factor to be unique to each transaction in most cases, and let banks use alternatives to SMS OTPs. Small contactless taps, UPI Lite and some recurring mandate debits are exempt. Common confusion: two passwords are not two factors. Never share an OTP; scammers ask for it because it is the second lock.
example: Say a fraudster steals your card number, expiry date and CVV and tries a ₹4,500 online purchase. Without the OTP sent to your phone, the payment fails. A 6-digit OTP has 10^6 = 10,00,000 possible values, so a single random guess has a 1 in 10 lakh chance of working.

short: Payments between people or businesses in different countries, such as remittances, import bills or card spending abroad, usually involving a currency conversion.
kid: Sending a birthday present to a cousin in another country takes longer and needs more stamps. Grown-ups are building faster roads so presents arrive sooner.
detail: Cross-border payments move money between countries: remittances home from workers abroad, payments for imports and exports, tuition fees, and card or UPI spending while travelling. Traditionally they pass through chains of correspondent banks holding nostro and vostro accounts and exchanging SWIFT messages, which makes them slow, expensive and hard to track. The G20 has set targets for 2027 to make them cheaper, faster and more transparent. One route is linking countries' fast payment systems: India's UPI was linked with Singapore's PayNow in 2023, and UPI is now accepted at merchants in countries such as the UAE, France, Nepal and Bhutan. India is the world's largest recipient of remittances, so costs here matter to millions of families. Common confusion: a zero-fee transfer is not free if the exchange rate offered is worse than the mid-market rate; the markup is the hidden fee.
example: Say a worker in the US sends $1,000 home and, for illustration, the mid-market rate is ₹87.00. Provider A charges no fee but converts at ₹86.00, delivering ₹86,000. Provider B charges a $5 fee and converts the remaining $995 at ₹86.80, delivering ₹86,366, so the 'free' transfer actually delivers ₹366 less.

short: A global standard for the format of financial messages, letting banks and payment systems exchange richer, structured data about each payment.
kid: If every friend writes party invitations the same neat way, with name, day and place in the same boxes, nobody gets confused. This is that neat way of writing, for the places that look after people's coins.
detail: ISO 20022 is an international standard, first published by the International Organization for Standardization in 2004, that defines a common vocabulary and XML-based message formats for payments, securities, trade finance and cards. Its big advantage over older formats is rich, structured data: separate fields for names, full addresses, purpose codes and invoice references instead of short free-text boxes. That makes it easier to match payments to invoices automatically, screen for sanctions and fraud, and analyse payment flows. Major systems have migrated: the euro area's T2 and the UK's CHAPS in 2023, Fedwire in the US in 2025, and SWIFT's cross-border payment messages after a coexistence period that ended in November 2025. India's RTGS has used it since its 2013 upgrade. Common confusion: it is a message format, not a payment network or a currency, so labelling certain cryptocurrencies as ISO 20022 coins is marketing, not a meaningful certification.
example: Older SWIFT MT messages fit a payer's name and address into four lines of 35 characters, just 4 x 35 = 140 characters, often cutting off details. Say a company receives 500 payments a month and staff match 10% of them, or 50, by hand because invoice references are truncated; if richer ISO 20022 data cuts that to 2%, only 10 need a human.
